beforeEvidence.text: I mean it burst, the long rubber line from the crock to the carboy, split along its belly with a crack like a shot, and a rope of yeast slurry went up and out and came down over all four of us. That is the last time I ever trust a rubber hose that came out of a barn.

So we went out with the beer. I want to be precise about this. I did not climb out of that cellar with dignity. I surfed out of it on my back in a brown wave, holding the carboy to my chest with both arms like a man carrying a baby out of a fire, and I came up the steps and out the hatch and into the lane on a tide of my own product.

They weren't chasing us. That's the thing nobody will believe. A hundred and thirty of them were in the lane, and they were on their knees in the spilled wort, lapping, fighting, rolling, and a few of them had gone flat on their backs in it and were making noises like happy dogs. But a dozen had come up the back of the wave, and those dozen were between us and the truck, and Pip was coming down the silo ladder, and one of the dozen — the man in the feed cap, back for more — turned and looked at Pip, who was wearing a coat two sizes too big and a climbing harness and nothing else that would save her.

So: the truck's gone, sunk in the mash pit with a hundred gallons of malt on it and a full tank of diesel we can't reach. The worm gear's gone. The rig's gone. Our position in the lane is gone, and by morning the horde will have drunk the pit dry and started making rounds again.

But the carboy's in my lap. The foil's on it, the stopper's in it, and the yeast inside is alive — I can see it working, that slow brown churn, the same churn my mother's jug made and my mother's mother's before that. Whatever else the county lost tonight, the line goes on.

I sat with the jar in my arms and watched the flashlight move in the lane, and the dead men drinking in the dark where my brewery used to be, and I thought: two nights' work, and it's half done, and it's cost us the truck and a night and a very good hose. That's the arithmetic. That's always the arithmetic.

observation.impact: Draft lines 53 and 55 quote 1.1(b)(iii) as making 'ownership of a thread' permanent and non-shared, while 1.1(d)(iv) gives the crowd 'credit for all statements within a thread,' reassignable hourly. Draft line 59 then treats these as the same claim ('A thread belongs permanently... And a thread belongs to whoever the crowd decides hourly'), and line 65 uses that as the direct contradiction the narrator will test. The draft’s own rule text, and line 13’s example of OP owning a thread while a reply gets the upvotes, distinguish thread ownership from credit for statements. Under the same actor and time, OP can own the thread permanently while the crowd holds or reassigns credit for statements; the two quoted clauses are therefore compatible, not directly contradictory. The chapter 2 intent requires the chapter to discover a direct contradiction between two binding sub-rules, so the text cannot both define these as different properties and establish the required contradiction.

beforeEvidence.text: Sub-rule 1.1(b)(iii): "Sovereignty is permanent. Ownership of a thread may not be transferred, revoked, or shared, and in the event of conflict with any other sub-rule, this clause prevails."
Sub-rule 1.1(d)(iv): "Credit for all statements within a thread belongs to the crowd, which may reassign it hourly; in the event of conflict with any other sub-rule, this clause prevails."

A thread belongs permanently to whoever posted first. And a thread belongs to whoever the crowd decides hourly. At the same time. Forever. Both binding. Both prevail. Two absolute claims in one document, in one subsection, and the Committee has not marked either as provisional, which it did for a footnote about lurkers that has been pending since v2.9.

Tomorrow, 9 a.m. I am going to post the exact same sentence into two threads. In the first, I will be the original poster and the sentence will be stupid. In the second, I will arrive late and the sentence will be identical and the sentence will still be stupid. Under 1.1(b) I own the first thread forever. Under 1.1(d) the crowd owns both from the first hour. One of these clauses will have to give, and the Committee will have to tell me which one in a way that is timestamped and witnessed by at least three strangers who do not like me. If they cannot, then I have found the seam.
